title: Judges Household Religion and Regional Cult Sites
summary: A passage-linked evidence cluster for Judges 17–18 and 21 that distinguishes the text's household shrine, hired priest, Danite cult installation, and Shiloh sanctuary setting from archaeological comparisons with Iron I regional cult places.
historical_context: Religious activity in Iron I was not confined to one architectural form or social scale. Biblical texts and archaeology preserve evidence for household, town, open-air, and regional sacred settings, but the evidence sets cannot simply be mapped onto one another.
ancient_near_east_context: Households across the Levant were economic, kinship, and religious units. Cult objects, local priestly service, votive practice, sacrifice, and festival travel could operate at different scales within the same wider religious landscape.
hebraic_worldview: Judges 17 portrays Micah expecting benefit from YHWH after installing a Levite, yet the narrator embeds the episode in the refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. The text describes religious reasoning while also directing readers to evaluate it critically.
canonical_context: Judges 17–18 presents a household cult that becomes a tribal installation at Dan, while Judges 21 locates an annual festival at Shiloh. Joshua, Samuel, Kings, Psalms, and Jeremiah preserve other stages in the canonical memory of Shiloh and Dan.
literary_context: The two closing narrative complexes of Judges move from private wrongdoing to tribal and intertribal disorder. Micah's shrine is appropriated and institutionalized by Dan, and the Shiloh festival is exploited to repair the consequences of civil war.
covenantal_significance: The cluster clarifies the social forms of the worship described in Judges while leaving the book's covenant critique intact. Description of a shrine, priest, image, or festival is not approval of the actions surrounding it.
intertextuality: Joshua 18 places the tent of meeting and land allotment at Shiloh.
First Samuel 1-4 remembers Shiloh as a sanctuary and as the setting of judgment on Eli's house.
First Kings 12:25-33 gives Dan a later royal-cult role distinct from the Judges 18 installation.
Psalm 78:60 and Jeremiah 7:12-14 invoke Shiloh as a warning about rejected sacred space.
timeline: Iron I regional religious settings: approximately 1200-1000 BCE
Narrated period of Judges 17-21: before monarchy; absolute chronology disputed
Shiloh excavations discussed here: campaigns of 1981-1984

interpretive_notes.note: Micah's expectation of prosperity is textually explicit, but reconstructing a universal Israelite household theology from one negatively framed narrative would exceed the evidence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: A narrative character's stated reasoning is evidence for characterization and possible social logic, not a statistical survey or normative doctrine.

interpretive_notes.note: Neither an Iron I open cult place nor occupation remains at Shiloh can by themselves be identified with Micah's shrine, the Danite installation, the tent of meeting, or the festival of Judges 21.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Comparable period and religious function do not establish identity with a named biblical installation or event.

evidence_items.title: Micah's household cult and expectation of divine favor
evidence_items.description: Judges 17 describes a household shrine with an image, ephod, teraphim, and priest, and reports Micah's expectation that installing a Levite will cause YHWH to prosper him.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The objects and Micah's statement are explicit, but interpreting their wider social prevalence or complete religious logic requires caution.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The evidence identifies the household scale and benefit-oriented reasoning of Micah's actions while preserving the narrator's negative no-king frame.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Micah establishes a shrine, makes or possesses named cult objects, appoints priests, and explicitly links the Levite's priesthood with expected good from YHWH.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: The episode can illuminate household patronage and expectations of divine benefit, but its literary framing warns against treating Micah as a normative spokesman or representative of every household.

evidence_items.title: Danite seizure and relocation of a household shrine
evidence_items.description: Judges 18 narrates Danite seizure of Micah's cult objects and Levite, followed by installation of the image and priestly line at Dan.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The movement from household possession to tribal installation is explicit in the narrative; no archaeological identification is asserted.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The episode shows how private religious property and patronage become a durable tribal cult arrangement within the book's account of Danite migration.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Danite scouts recognize the priestly voice, the migrating force takes the cult objects and Levite, and the tribe sets up the image at Dan.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Commentators emphasize the narrative's escalation from household disorder to institutionalized tribal worship and distinguish it from Dan's later royal sanctuary.

evidence_items.title: Shiloh sanctuary and annual festival setting
evidence_items.description: Judges refers to the house of God at Shiloh and gives a precise route description for an annual festival of YHWH there; excavation documents occupation but does not identify the narrated installations or event.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The textual role and site occupation are supported, but the date, form, and archaeological location of the sanctuary and festival remain uncertain.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The evidence grounds Judges 21 in a named regional gathering place while preventing occupation remains from being treated as proof of the festival or tabernacle.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Judges 18:31 names the house of God at Shiloh, and Judges 21:19 locates an annual festival through a detailed description relative to Bethel, Lebonah, and a road.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: Shiloh functioned in Israelite memory as a regional sanctuary, but archaeology has not securely identified the tent of meeting or the event narrated in Judges 21.

evidence_items.title: Bull Site as an Iron I open-cult-place comparison
evidence_items.description: The Bull Site is published as a small Iron I open cult place with a bronze bull figurine; its users, deity, and relationship to named biblical communities are not securely identifiable.
evidence_items.confidence_rationale: The site and assemblage are documented, but interpretation of cultic identity, ethnicity, and specific religious meaning remains disputed.
evidence_items.passage_relevance: The site offers a period comparison for cult activity outside a monumental urban temple while providing no warrant to identify it with Micah, Dan, Shiloh, or a narrated event.
evidence_items.primary_observation: Excavation documented an Iron I hilltop enclosure and a bronze bull figurine in a context published as an open cult place.
evidence_items.scholarly_interpretation: The assemblage is widely discussed in reconstructions of Iron I religion, but proposals about the site's community and the figurine's divine associations remain inferential.
